part2.intro: Three young people talk about a time when there was no electricity in their home.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Lena
texts.text: Last winter there was a big storm and we had no electricity for two whole days. There was no heating, so we were all freezing! We slept in the living room together under lots of blankets. Luckily our cooker uses gas, so Mum could still make hot soup for everyone. In the evenings we listened to an old radio with batteries and played cards. It was actually quite fun.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Kenji
texts.text: It happened in July while I was writing a story for English on the computer. Suddenly the screen went black and I lost everything because I hadn't saved it. I had to write it all again! The electricity came back after six hours, but by then the fridge was warm and we had to throw away all the ice cream. Now I always save my work every five minutes.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Thu
texts.text: The lights went off in the middle of my thirteenth birthday party! At first everyone screamed, but then my friends turned on the lights on their mobile phones so we could see. My dad brought in the cake with the candles burning, and it looked really beautiful in the dark. We couldn't play any music, so we sang songs instead. It was the best party ever.

items.q: Who lost some work they were doing?
Whose family could still cook a hot meal?
Who says people used phones so they could see?
Who does something differently now because of what happened?
Who had no electricity for more than one day?
Who was celebrating something when the electricity went off?
Who was unhappy about some food?

part3.title: The girl who fixes things
part3.text:
Every second Saturday, a classroom at Hilltop School becomes a busy workshop. People arrive with broken lamps, radios, hairdryers and CD players, and thirteen-year-old Sofia Marino and her team try to repair them for free.

Sofia first became interested in fixing things when she was nine. "My mum is an engineer, and she let me help her when she repaired our old clock," she says. "People think I learned from videos on the internet, but Mum taught me almost everything."

The idea for the Repair Club came last year. "Our neighbour put a nearly new DVD player in the rubbish because it didn't work," Sofia explains. "I took it home and it only needed a new cable. It cost two pounds to fix! I thought, why do people throw so many things away?"

The club has some important rules. "We only repair small things that people can carry," says Sofia. "We never touch anything that uses gas, and we don't do big things like fridges or cookers. That's a job for experts."

The first meeting wasn't easy. "Only three people came, and we couldn't fix any of their things!" Sofia laughs. "So I put a poster in the supermarket, and now we have twenty or thirty visitors every time." Five friends from her class help her, and a science teacher checks that everything is safe before people take it home.

What's next? "I'd love to start clubs like this at other schools in our town," Sofia says. "Then fewer things will end up in the rubbish."

a science teacher at her school

options: Her neighbour asked her to repair his DVD player.

part4.title: Before the fridge
part4.text:
Today it is hard to imagine a kitchen without a fridge, but for most of history people had to find other ways to {19} their food cold. Some families kept meat and milk in a cool room under the house. Others bought large pieces of ice, which were cut from frozen lakes in winter and {20} in special buildings until the summer.

The first electric fridges for homes went on {21} in the USA in the 1910s. They were very expensive – one cost more than a car – so only rich families had them. Early fridges also used gases that could make people very {22}.

By the 1950s, fridges were cheaper and safer, and most homes in the USA had one. In many other countries, people had to {23} until the 1970s or even later.

Modern fridges use much less electricity than older ones. Some of them can even tell you when you have {24} out of milk!

items.q: What did the girl buy at the shop?

script.t: Hi Zoe. What did you get at the shops? Did you buy that new hairdryer?
No, it was too expensive. I'll wait for the sale.
Oh. So what's in the bag?
There was a lovely clock, but I've already got one in my room. So I bought a lamp for my desk. Now I can read in the evenings.

items.q: What time will the man come to repair the heating?

script.t: Sam, the man from the heating company phoned. He can't come at ten o'clock tomorrow.
Oh no. Is he coming later? I'm home at half past eleven.
No, he's coming earlier, at half past eight. I'll be here, so you can go to school as usual.
Great. I'm so tired of being cold!

items.q: What is the family going to buy for the kitchen?

script.t: Mum, are we getting a new cooker? Ours is really old.
It's old, but it still works well. The problem is the fridge. It makes a terrible noise and the milk isn't cold any more.
So we're buying a new one?
Yes, on Saturday. Dad wants a radio for the kitchen too, but that can wait until next month.

items.q: How did the boy watch the football match?

script.t: Did you see the match last night, Ali? Did you watch it on your big TV?
No, my brother was watching a film on it, and he wouldn't change the channel.
What about your laptop?
I left it at my grandad's. So I watched it on my phone. The screen was so small, but at least I saw the goals!

items.q: What does the boy's grandfather like doing most in the evenings?

script.t: Does your grandad watch a lot of TV in the evenings, Jamie?
Only the news. Then he turns it off.
Does he watch films? He's got lots of DVDs, hasn't he?
He never watches them! What he really loves is sitting in his armchair and listening to his old jazz CDs.

part2.intro: You will hear a woman talking to a group of students at a museum.
part2.title: The Museum of Home Technology

items.label: The oldest thing in the museum is a:
In the photography room, students can use an old:
To book another school visit, contact: Mrs

script.t: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Museum of Home Technology. Here you can see how people lived before computers and mobile phones. Lots of visitors think the oldest thing in our museum is the radio in the first room, but it isn't. It's a telephone from eighteen ninety, and you'll find it near the main stairs. Now, if you're interested in cooking, the old kitchen machines, like the first electric cookers and fridges, are in Room eight. Room nine has televisions and video recorders from the nineteen sixties and seventies. My favourite place is the photography room. There, you can take a picture with a real camera from the nineteen fifties. You can't use your own phones in that room, I'm afraid. The museum closes at five o'clock, but the café closes earlier, at a quarter past four, so get your drinks before then. Finally, a message for your teachers. If your school would like to visit again, please contact Mrs Pryce. That's P-R-Y-C-E. She organises all our school visits. Right, let's start in the first room.

items.q: What will the school do with the money from the sale?
options: repair the heating in the gym
buy new laptops for the library

items.q: What is Ruby going to sell?
How much will Sam ask for his camera?
What job will Ruby do at the sale?
When will Sam bring his things to school?

script.t: Hi Sam. Are you bringing anything to the school sale on Saturday?
Maybe. What's the money for this year? Last year it paid for the class trip to London, didn't it?
That's right. This year they want to buy new laptops for the library. The heating in the gym is broken too, but the town is paying to repair that.
OK. So what are you selling?

Well, I wanted to sell my old MP3 player, but I still use it when I go running. And Grandad offered me his video recorder, but nobody has videos any more! So Dad's given me his DVD player. He watches everything online now.
I've got an old camera I never use. I thought I'd ask twelve pounds for it.
That's a lot. People only pay about five pounds for old cameras on the internet.
But mine has a really nice case. I'll ask for eight. That's fair.
Good idea.
Are you helping at the sale?
Yes. Mr Ford wanted me to take the money, but I'm terrible at maths! So I'm going to test all the electric things and make sure they work. The Year Seven students have already made the posters.
When should I bring my camera?
Mr Ford says Friday afternoon is best.
I've got football then. And Saturday morning is too late. I'll bring it on Thursday morning – Mum can drive me.

items.intro: You will hear a girl talking to her friend about a new hairdryer.
items.q: What does the girl think of her new hairdryer?

script.t: Is that your new hairdryer, Grace? It looks nice and light.
It is light, and it gets really hot, so my hair dries quickly.
So you're happy with it?
Not really. When I turn it on, it's so noisy that it wakes up my little brother. Mum isn't very pleased!

script.t: Hi Nadia, it's Josh. I'm really sorry, but I can't come to watch the film at your house tonight. My mum isn't well and I have to look after my little sister. Don't worry about the DVD I borrowed – I'll give it back to you at school tomorrow. Maybe we can watch something together at the weekend instead. Bye!

items.q: What does the mother want her son to do?

script.t: Leo, are you cold? You're only wearing a T-shirt.
A bit. Can I turn the heating up?
No, electricity is so expensive this winter. The windows are all closed, so go and get your sweater from your room, please.
OK, Mum.

items.intro: You will hear a teacher talking to her class at the start of a lesson.
items.q: What will the lesson be about?
options: how electricity gets to our homes

script.t: Good morning, class. Last week we learned how batteries work, and next week we'll talk about how we can save electricity at home. But today I want to show you something different. When you switch on the lights or the TV, where does the electricity come from? How does it travel all the way to your house? Let's watch this short video and find out.

items.intro: You will hear a girl talking about staying with her grandparents.
items.q: How does the girl feel when she stays there?

script.t: My grandparents live on a farm, and they don't have a TV or a computer. There's just an old telephone in the kitchen. My friends think I must be bored there, but I'm not at all. I sleep really well, I go for long walks with Grandpa, and I help Grandma in the garden. And there are always lots of people around. I feel so calm when I'm there.

part5.intro: You will hear Nick talking to his mum about a family holiday. What is each person taking on holiday?

script.t: Mum, is Dad taking his laptop on holiday? He always says he has to work.
Not this time! I told him no work on holiday, so the laptop's staying at home. He's taking his camera instead. He wants to take lots of pictures of the mountains.
Good. What about Grandma? Is she bringing her CD player? She loves her music.
She wanted to, but there isn't space in the car. She's only bringing her little travel clock. She never uses the alarm on her phone – she says it's too difficult.
And Lily? I bet she's taking her MP3 player.
It's broken, actually. But she's packed her hairdryer. She says there won't be one at the cottage.
Is cousin Ben coming with us in the car?
Yes, and it's a long journey for a six-year-old. So his mum's giving us her small DVD player. He can watch cartoons in the back of the car.
That's a good idea. Can I take something too?
Of course. What do you want to take?
There's no TV at the cottage, so I'm taking my radio. Then I can listen to the football results on Saturday.
